sections.html: The dwarf aquarium lily (Nymphaea stellata) is an easy-to-grow species from India and Southeast Asia, often used as a midground or background plant. Its bulb sprouts a compact bush of 4-inch (about 10 cm), arrow-shaped leaves and eventually extends long stems with lily pads that float at the water surface. Leaf colours range from reddish-bronze to pinkish-green.

This hardy plant grows in a wide range of tropical temperatures from 22-28°C (72-82°F). It doesn't require CO2 injection and can live in aquariums with low to high lighting.

Once it starts sending lily pads to the top, you may need to prune a few of the surface leaves so they won't block light from reaching other plants. Trim back some (but not all) of the lily pads if they begin to cover the entire surface of the water.

Dwarf aquarium lilies, like most live aquatic plants, are great for consuming organic waste compounds and improving overall water quality. However, once established, lilies tend to grow quickly and may need additional nutrients in the form of liquid fertilizers and root tabs.

Planting

The plant is sold as a potted plant with a bulb. It may arrive with a few leaves, but they are delicate and often damaged in transit. More leaves grow about a week to 10 days after planting. Remove the rock wool from the plastic basket, gently split it into two halves to free the bulb, and carefully remove the bulb.

Place the bulb on top of the substrate with the leaves facing upward and the roots pointing down. Do not bury the entire bulb. It may float at first, but will sink once soaked. The roots will eventually grow into the substrate and hold the bulb in place. Once the lily has sprouted leaves, you can push the bulb slightly into the substrate without covering any new shoots.

Fuzzy growth on the bulb

Organic objects such as driftwood or plant bulbs underwater often grow a layer of biofilm made of harmless bacteria and other microorganisms. It can look like white mold, fluffy fungus or short tufts of gray hair. Algae eaters, shrimp or snails will often eat it. As long as the bulb is firm and eventually sprouts, the biofilm is not dangerous to the lily and doesn't spread to other plants.

Propagation

When the plant is feeding and growing well, it may send out small shoots with daughter plants attached. Cut off the side shoots and replant them where desired. If the plant is not thriving, it may have a nutrient deficiency.
